name: Alerting
intent: Wake a person only when something needs a human right now, by alerting on symptoms users feel and on how fast the error budget is burning, not on every blip.
scenario: The on-call engineer is paged at 3 a.m. for a one-minute spike that fixed itself. The following week a slow, real incident runs for two hours and no alert fires at all.
problem: Alerts that fire too often teach people to ignore them (alert fatigue), and burn out the on-call. Alerts that are too relaxed miss real incidents. Naive rules, such as 'error rate above 1% in any minute', are both: noisy on short blips and blind to slow, steady problems.

howItWorks.title: Alert on symptoms, not causes
howItWorks.text: Page when users are affected: high error rate, slow responses, failing key journeys. High CPU or a full disk on one server is a cause that may or may not hurt anyone. Cause-level signals belong on dashboards or in tickets, unless they predict an imminent user-facing failure.

howItWorks.title: Every page must be urgent, actionable and new
howItWorks.text: Ask of each alert: does it need a human now, is there something concrete to do, and does it tell them something they do not already know? If not, it should be a ticket, a dashboard panel or deleted. Each alert should link to a runbook explaining the first steps.

howItWorks.title: Require the condition to persist
howItWorks.text: A 'for 5 minutes' clause means a one-minute spike does not page anyone. It trades a little detection delay for far fewer false pages. Pick the duration from how long an outage must last before it matters.

howItWorks.title: Use burn rate against the SLO
howItWorks.text: Compare the current error rate to the rate that would spend the whole error budget exactly on time. A fast burn (for example 14 times the allowed rate over an hour) pages someone, a slow burn (6 times over six hours) opens a ticket. Using two windows catches both sudden outages and quiet leaks.

howItWorks.title: Review alerts regularly
howItWorks.text: Track how many pages happened, how many needed action, and who got woken up. Delete alerts that never lead to action, tune the noisy ones, and add alerts after every incident that was found by a customer instead of by monitoring.

pros: People are woken up rarely, and only for real problems
Burn-rate alerts tie paging to what users and the business care about
Fewer, better alerts keep on-call sustainable
cons: Tuning takes iteration and ongoing care
A 'for' duration delays detection by design
Needs reliable metrics and an SLO to work well
Too few alerts risks missing something, too many causes fatigue
whenToUse: Every production service with real users
Page for urgent user-facing problems, ticket for slow burns and capacity trends
whenNotToUse: Alerting on every error or every resource threshold
Pages that nobody can act on, such as an upstream outage you cannot influence (show it on a dashboard instead)
pitfalls: Alerts with no runbook, so the on-call has to start from scratch at 3 a.m.
Ignoring alerts that 'always fire', until one of them is real
A single threshold on a noisy metric with no duration
Alerts that depend on the same system that is failing, so they fail silently with it
